Priority gaps and improvement actions

Shown in a provisional display order: answers scored 0 first, then 1, then Unknown, each in indicator order. This is not a validated ranking of impact or urgency. The actions are general prompts based on your answers, not findings about the site.

Gap 1.3 — Link to grey infrastructure (Score 0 / 2)
Finding
NBS are planned separately from drainage, roads and buildings, or not linked to them at all.
Why it matters
NBS planned with drainage, roads and buildings are cheaper to build, easier to maintain and more likely to work as intended.
Suggested action
Introduce a step in infrastructure projects to consider NBS at the design stage.
Evidence needed
Project design documents, drainage or road plans and procedures for infrastructure projects.
Gap 2.3 — Targets and monitoring (Score 0 / 2)
Finding
No measurable NBS targets exist.
Why it matters
Measurable targets and regular reporting show whether NBS are progressing and allow plans to be corrected.
Suggested action
Define a small set of measurable NBS targets, for example area, number or condition of solutions, with a baseline year.
Evidence needed
Target statements, monitoring indicators and progress reports.
Gap 5.2 — Long-term maintenance budget (Score 0 / 2)
Finding
No budget covers maintenance, watering or replacement of NBS.
Why it matters
NBS need continuing care. Without it they can fail within a few years.
Suggested action
Prepare an operation and maintenance budget and clarify who is responsible for funding it.
Evidence needed
Maintenance plans, annual budget lines and financial documentation.
Gap 5.3 — Co-benefits valued in decisions (Score 0 / 2)
Finding
Co-benefits such as cooling, health and flood protection are not counted in funding decisions.
Why it matters
Counting co-benefits can strengthen the case for funding NBS compared with grey alternatives.
Suggested action
Include a short co-benefit description in funding proposals and business cases.
Evidence needed
Funding proposals, business cases and any co-benefit studies.
Partial 1.1 — NBS inventory (Score 1 / 2)
Finding
An inventory exists but is incomplete or needs updating.
Why it matters
Without a record of what exists, the area cannot plan, maintain or build on its NBS.
Suggested action
Update and complete the inventory so that it covers the whole area and records type, location and condition.
Evidence needed
GIS inventories, municipal records or site documentation.

The actions are general prompts based on your answers, not findings about the site. # Indicator Type Finding Why it matters Suggested action Evidence needed 1 1.3 — Link to grey infrastructure Gap NBS are planned separately from drainage, roads and buildings, or not linked to them at all. NBS planned with drainage, roads and buildings are cheaper to build, easier to maintain and more likely to work as intended. Introduce a step in infrastructure projects to consider NBS at the design stage. Project design documents, drainage or road plans and procedures for infrastructure projects. 2 2.3 — Targets and monitoring Gap No measurable NBS targets exist. Measurable targets and regular reporting show whether NBS are progressing and allow plans to be corrected. Define a small set of measurable NBS targets, for example area, number or condition of solutions, with a baseline year. Target statements, monitoring indicators and progress reports. 3 5.2 — Long-term maintenance budget Gap No budget covers maintenance, watering or replacement of NBS. NBS need continuing care. Without it they can fail within a few years. Prepare an operation and maintenance budget and clarify who is responsible for funding it. Maintenance plans, annual budget lines and financial documentation. 4 5.3 — Co-benefits valued in decisions Gap Co-benefits such as cooling, health and flood protection are not counted in funding decisions. Counting co-benefits can strengthen the case for funding NBS compared with grey alternatives. Include a short co-benefit description in funding proposals and business cases. Funding proposals, business cases and any co-benefit studies. 5 1.1 — NBS inventory Partial An inventory exists but is incomplete or needs updating. Without a record of what exists, the area cannot plan, maintain or build on its NBS. Update and complete the inventory so that it covers the whole area and records type, location and condition. GIS inventories, municipal records or site documentation. 6 1.2 — Coverage of public space Partial Some public space has green or blue features, but coverage is partial or uneven, or falls short of a local target where one exists. Coverage shows how much of the public space can already contribute to cooling, shade and water management. Identify the districts with low or uneven coverage and compare coverage with a local target, or agree on one. Land-cover or green-space maps, municipal green-area statistics and any local target. 7 2.1 — NBS in strategic plans Partial NBS are mentioned in some plans, but without specific measures, locations or responsibilities. NBS that are named in plans, with measures and responsibilities, are more likely to be funded and delivered. Add specific measures, locations and responsible bodies for NBS to the plans that mention them. The text of the applicable plans, with the sections that mention NBS. 8 2.2 — Regulation and standards Partial Some rules or standards encourage NBS, but they are voluntary, partial or rarely applied. Rules and incentives make NBS a normal part of development, not a voluntary extra. Clarify and apply the existing rules or incentives more consistently, and track how often they are applied. Zoning regulations, building codes, green-area standards and examples of their application. 9 3.1 — Dedicated staff or unit Partial Staff handle NBS alongside other duties, or responsibility is limited to one department. Clear responsibility keeps NBS on the agenda and avoids tasks falling between departments. Formalise the role and extend its mandate across departments. Organisation charts, job descriptions or a decision naming the responsible unit. 10 3.2 — Technical know-how Partial Some experience or guidance exists, but it is limited to certain NBS types or relies on outside support. Technical know-how decides whether NBS are built well and kept working over time. Extend skills and guidance to further NBS types and reduce reliance on outside support. Examples of delivered projects, guidance documents and staff or contractor qualifications. 11 4.1 — Community participation Partial Residents are consulted, but mostly after the main decisions have been made. Early participation improves fit with local needs and support for upkeep. Move participation to an earlier stage so residents can influence priorities and design. Workshop or consultation records, and records of how input changed decisions. 12 4.2 — Coordination across departments and owners Partial Coordination happens case by case, or only between some of the actors. Many NBS depend on land, assets or budgets held by different actors. Turn case-by-case coordination into a regular mechanism, such as a standing working group. Meeting records, agreements between actors or a working-group mandate. 13 5.1 — Capital funding Partial Some funding is secured or likely, but it does not cover the planned NBS. Without capital funding, planned NBS stay on paper. Close the funding gap for the planned NBS by securing additional sources or phasing the works. Budget documents, grant agreements and funding commitments. 14 3.3 — Data and monitoring tools To verify No information is available for this indicator yet. This is a gap in information, not evidence of weak performance. Data are needed to place NBS where they help most and to check whether they work. Obtain or verify this information before drawing conclusions. Dataset lists, data-sharing agreements and examples of data used in decisions. How the rule-based match score is calculated (provisional) Each option has a weight from 0 (not a target) to 3 (strong) for heatwaves, flooding and drought. These are the earlier demo weights, kept as provisional rules pending methodology review. They have not been validated by PROMEA. Matching rules for Coastal Storms and Land Degradation have not been defined. When either is selected, or when Not Sure is selected, no match score or ranking is produced. Score = sum of the weights for your selected risks, divided by 3 times the number of selected risks, times 100. Land context: 15 points are subtracted for each level by which the option's land need exceeds the public land available, and 10 more points when urban density is high and the land need is high. The score is limited to 0 to 100. Urban density and public land availability are qualitative answers, not numerical thresholds. If public land availability is Unknown, no match score is produced. Institutional gaps (funding, maintenance, technical know-how) are not used to change the score. They are shown as implementation conditions. Climate type is not yet used in matching. It will be considered once verified location-specific information and decision rules are available. Public land availability is not used as evidence that a roof is available. Roofs are checked separately in the applicability checks. Screening: an option is Not applicable only when a basic condition is answered No (for example no roof, no coast, no runoff source). Unknown, or a No on a condition that can be assessed or designed (for example structural suitability), gives Requires verification.
